title: India Is Sending 120 Deeptech Startups to France. It Is the Country’s Biggest Innovation Bet Yet.
excerpt: Bharat Innovates 2026 will showcase chips, biotech, quantum, and clean energy ventures in Nice — timed to Modi’s G7 visit and the India-France Year of Innovation.
body:
India is sending 120 of its most promising deeptech startups to Nice, France, for the first edition of Bharat Innovates 2026 — a government-backed showcase timed to coincide with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to France for the G7 summit and a bilateral meeting with President Emmanuel Macron.

The event, scheduled for June 14–16, is organized by India’s Ministry of Education in partnership with France and sits inside the India-France Year of Innovation that Modi and Macron jointly launched in Mumbai on February 17. It represents the most ambitious single deployment of Indian startups on a global stage to date.

## Not a Trade Mission — A Structured Accelerator

Bharat Innovates is not a conventional trade delegation. The three-day programme at the Palais des Expositions in Nice includes startup pitches organized by sector, roundtables with international investors and manufacturers, co-development workshops, and targeted networking sessions.

The 120 startups were selected through a rigorous multi-stage evaluation process from over 3,000 initial applications. All are linked to higher education institutions or centrally funded technical institutes such as IITs and NITs. A pre-summit held at IIT Bombay in March served as the national showcase before the cohort’s international debut.

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has described the initiative as “a national innovation movement and a global platform for collaboration.” Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri called it one of India’s key initiatives in technology, higher education, research, and development.

## What India Is Bringing

The cohort reflects a fundamental shift in India’s startup ecosystem. For years, software and consumer internet companies dominated. The Bharat Innovates cohort is overwhelmingly hardware, industrial systems, and scientific technology.

Biotech and healthtech make up the largest category with 24 startups, including Dozee, Eka Care, String Bio, and SigTuple. Clean energy and climate tech contribute 12 ventures, including AmpereHour Energy and Kazam EV Tech. Semiconductors are represented by Mindgrove, Bharat Semi, and AGNIT.

The list also spans drones and aerospace, electric vehicles, robotics, defence technology, advanced manufacturing, and quantum computing. Companies like Ather Energy, Ultraviolette, CynLr, Kalam Labs, and QNu Labs are building physical products and foundational technologies — chips, batteries, autonomous systems, and quantum communication infrastructure.

India now has over 200,000 recognized startups and more than 120 unicorns, supported by roughly 1.5 million engineers trained annually. The Bharat Innovates cohort is meant to demonstrate that the country’s innovation capacity extends well beyond software services.

## The Strategic Timing

The event begins on June 14, one day before the G7 summit formally opens. That timing gives Indian founders a rare window to meet global capital alongside one of the year’s most important diplomatic gatherings.

The India-France bilateral relationship has expanded significantly in recent years, encompassing defence, civil nuclear energy, space, climate action, and digital technology. Innovation is now positioned as the newest pillar. Modi’s presence at the G7 — India is not a member but is frequently invited as a guest — adds diplomatic weight to what might otherwise be a sector-specific event.

For France, the appeal is clear: access to India’s deep bench of engineering talent and a pipeline of startups working on problems — energy storage, healthcare diagnostics, semiconductor design — that Europe needs solved. For India, it is a chance to position its startups as global contenders rather than domestic success stories.

## What Comes Next

The immediate question is whether Bharat Innovates leads to concrete deals — joint ventures, technology licensing agreements, investment commitments — or remains a high-profile showcase. The government has signalled that this is meant to be an annual initiative, with the Nice event serving as a proof of concept.

For the 120 founders making the trip, the stakes are personal. Many are building capital-intensive hardware businesses that require the kind of patient, deep-pocketed investors that remain scarce in India. If Nice delivers those connections, Bharat Innovates could become the most significant bridge between Indian innovation and global markets since the IT services boom of the 2000s.

*Sources: YourStory, Press Information Bureau, Startup Feed, AInvest*
